claims.text: Depositing an epitaxial FeCoNi–platinum-group-metal high-entropy-alloy shell onto Pd nanocubes alters the catalyst surface electronic structure.
The epitaxial high-entropy-alloy shell induces lattice strain.
The shell-induced electronic and strain effects weaken adsorbate binding energies.
Weaker adsorbate binding caused by the shell improves catalytic activity relative to bare Pd nanocubes.
The high-entropy-alloy shell improves catalyst durability relative to bare Pd nanocubes.
The deposited high-entropy-alloy shell grows coherently on the Pd nanocubes.
The coherently grown shell modulates the d-band electronic structure of the catalyst surface.
The epitaxial shell modifies the d-band center of the Pd core.
Modification of the d-band center alters the binding energies of reaction intermediates.
Altered intermediate binding optimizes the adsorption–desorption balance.
Optimization of the adsorption–desorption balance enhances catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
Coated catalysts will exhibit measurable XAS spectral shifts relative to bare Pd nanocubes.
The predicted XAS spectral shifts would indicate an altered d-band center.
DFT will predict lower adsorbate binding energies for coated catalysts than for bare Pd nanocubes.
Coated catalysts will have a higher turnover frequency than bare Pd nanocubes under identical reaction conditions.
Coated catalysts will have better product selectivity than bare Pd nanocubes under identical reaction conditions.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to reactions whose behavior is sensitive to adsorbate binding energies.
The hypothesis may not apply under extreme conditions where structural degradation dominates.
Electronic-structure shifts and kinetic changes may vary with reaction conditions and alloy composition.
A joint absence of measurable electronic-structure changes and catalytic-performance improvements relative to bare Pd would falsify the hypothesis.
